verdict.reasoning: Patient reports a terrible headache since midday on the left side with nausea and feeling like needing to vomit, and later states, “Yeah, I vomited twice.”
Headache is described as “throbbing on that left side” and worsens “if I lean forward or like move my head or neck. Yeah, the headache gets worse.”
Patient says, “I noticed some zigzag lines in my vision. A few minutes before the headache started, my vision blurred… It feels like it's on both [eyes].”
Doctor asks about bright lights and patient replies, “Yeah, well, I'm wearing, wearing sunglasses right now. You know, light's really hurting my eyes,” indicating photophobia and use of sunglasses.
In response to vomiting, patient states, “Yeah, I vomited twice.”
Doctor asks, “Any temperatures or fevers?” and patient responds, “No, I don't feel feverish.”
Doctor asks if the pain came on suddenly or gradual; patient answers, “No, really, it just happened,” indicating sudden onset, not gradual.
Patient says, “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago.” When asked duration, patient replies, “For a couple of days.”
Patient denies speech problems (“No.”), limb numbness or weakness (“No.”), and balance/coordination problems (“No.”).
Patient notes headache is “worse when I move” and with moving head/neck; no relieving factors are mentioned in relation to the current episode.
Doctor asks about head injuries: “Have you had a fall recently or been knocked on the head?” Patient responds, “No.”
Patient says, “Not really prone to them, no. But I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago,” and when asked about past migraines: “No.”
Patient states, “I take the pill, microgynon.” When asked duration: “Three months.” And confirms it is “for contraception.”
The transcript contains no discussion of drug allergies, so stating that no drug allergies are noted introduces undocumented information.
Patient says, “My mum had. Has migraines, but I've not been diagnosed.”
Patient states, “My mum has an underactive thyroid as well.”
When asked who is at home, patient replies, “I live on my own.”
Patient notes, “working fashion industry and you know, they're wondering what's going on,” and doctor later reiterates, “You mentioned you work in a fashion industry.”
Patient confirms job is stressful: “Yeah, it's really stressful, actually. Having problems with like people at work… managers like putting a lot of pressure on me.”
Doctor asks, “Do you smoke at all?” Patient answers, “No.”
Doctor asks, “And do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient responds, “No.”
As part of systems review, doctor asks about “temperatures or fevers” and patient replies, “No, I don't feel feverish.”
Doctor asks about head injuries (“Have you had a fall recently or been knocked on the head?”) and patient answers, “No,” documenting no head injury.

Doctor states, “I wonder whether you may have a migraine. Migraine type headache. It sounds very classical… The headache on one side, throbbing nature, the nausea, vomiting, sensitive to bright lights,” and patient had visual aura (zigzag lines, blurred vision) before onset.

No focal deficits are reported (speech, limb weakness, balance all denied), patient denies fever, and while neck movement worsens pain, neck stiffness as a meningeal sign is not reported; doctor says he is reassured it's not meningitis or brain cancer.
Doctor comments, “Certainly this is the second migraine you've had in the space of a month.”
Although work stress is discussed, the clinician does not explicitly state in the transcript that psychosocial stress is considered a contributing factor to the headache.
Doctor advises, “I think keeping a headache diary will be quite important to see exactly what's triggering these headaches.”
Doctor recommends “Some strong painkillers… paracetamol or even cocodamol and some anti inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen.”

Doctor says that if headaches become more persistent, “we can maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening in the first place. Something prophylactic medicines.”
Regarding Microgynon, doctor states, “That's something we may have a little discussion about today as well,” indicating a plan to discuss contraception in this context.
Doctor proposes follow-up: “we can have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps.”

Doctor instructs, “if your symptoms aren't getting better in the next two, three days, or indeed they're getting worse, I'd like you to come back and see me straight away… if your headache's getting worse… or your neck pain is getting worse, or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs or your vision, then I want you to come back and see me straight away.”
